written.myAnswer: In yeast, a small bud grows from the parent cell. The nucleus divides, and one daughter nucleus enters the bud. The bud grows and may detach to form a new yeast cell.
Fungi produce spores, often in sporangia. When mature, the spores are released and dispersed. In favourable conditions, they germinate and grow into new fungi.
Fungal spores can disperse and grow into new fungi in favourable conditions. Bacterial endospores help bacteria survive harsh conditions and resume growth when conditions improve.
A runner is a horizontal stem that grows above the ground. Roots and shoots develop at its nodes, forming new plants that can become independent of the parent.
A potato tuber is an underground modified stem with buds called eyes. The eyes sprout and produce shoots and roots that develop into a new plant.

Vegetative propagation is rapid, requires only one parent and preserves desirable parental traits. Its disadvantages include little genetic variation and the possible transmission of disease from parent to offspring.
The four whorls are the calyx (sepals), corolla (petals), androecium (stamens, each with an anther and filament), and gynoecium or carpel (stigma, style and ovary).

A megaspore mother cell in the ovule undergoes meiosis to form four megaspores. Usually three degenerate; the remaining one undergoes three mitotic divisions to form eight nuclei, including an egg cell and two polar nuclei.

Asexual reproduction involves one parent and no fusion of gametes, and usually produces genetically similar offspring. Sexual reproduction involves fusion of male and female gametes and produces genetic variation.

In bacteria, DNA replicates and the cell divides by binary fission; bacteria lack a true nucleus. In Amoeba, the nucleus divides first by mitosis, followed by division of the cytoplasm, usually in any plane.
A stolon is a horizontal aboveground stem; a rhizome is a horizontal underground stem.
A bulb has a short underground stem surrounded by fleshy scale leaves. A corm is a swollen underground stem covered by dry scale leaves.
In cutting, a piece of a plant develops roots and shoots to form a new plant. In grafting, a scion is joined to the rooted stock of another plant.

Vegetative propagation forms new plants from vegetative parts and may occur naturally or artificially. Artificial propagation is carried out by humans using methods such as cutting, grafting or layering.
The male gametophyte is the pollen grain, which produces male gametes. The female gametophyte is the embryo sac in the ovule, which contains the egg cell and polar nuclei.
The calyx is the outermost whorl and consists of sepals. The corolla lies inside it and consists of petals.
The stamen is the male reproductive part and consists of anther and filament. The carpel is the female reproductive part and consists of stigma, style and ovary.
Bacterial DNA replicates as the cell grows and elongates. The cell membrane and wall grow inward to form a septum, dividing the cell into two daughter bacteria.

Vegetative propagation is asexual reproduction in which new plants develop from vegetative parts of a parent. Structures used include runners (horizontal aboveground stems), rhizomes (horizontal underground stems), tubers (swollen underground stems with buds), bulbs (short stems with fleshy scale leaves) and corms (swollen underground stems with dry scale leaves).

Humans can grow plants by cutting, grafting and layering. In cutting, a piece of stem, root or leaf develops into a plant. In grafting, a scion is joined to a stock. In layering, a branch forms roots while attached to the parent, then is separated and planted.

The sporophyte is the diploid generation that produces haploid spores by meiosis. The gametophyte is the haploid generation that develops from a spore and produces gametes by mitosis. Fertilization forms a diploid zygote that develops into a sporophyte.

The dominant diploid sporophyte forms flowers. Meiosis produces haploid spores; microspores develop into pollen grains (male gametophytes), and a megaspore develops into the embryo sac (female gametophyte). After pollination, the pollen tube carries male gametes to the embryo sac. One fuses with the egg to form a diploid zygote, and the other fuses with the polar nuclei to form triploid endosperm. The zygote develops into an embryo, and the ovule becomes a seed that can germinate into a new sporophyte.

A diploid megaspore mother cell in the ovule undergoes meiosis to form four haploid megaspores. Usually three degenerate. The functional megaspore undergoes three mitotic divisions to form eight nuclei, which arrange into a seven-celled embryo sac: an egg and two synergids at one end, three antipodals at the other, and a central cell with two polar nuclei.
Many spores have protective coverings and can remain dormant, helping them withstand harsh conditions such as dryness or extreme temperatures. They can germinate when conditions become favourable.

Asexual reproduction usually produces genetically similar offspring and creates little variation. Sexual reproduction combines genetic material from gametes, producing varied offspring and increasing genetic diversity.

A pollen grain on a compatible stigma germinates and forms a pollen tube. The tube grows down the style into the ovary and enters an ovule, carrying male gametes to the embryo sac for double fertilization.
